lesson.title: Terraform building blocks: providers, resources, data sources and modules
lesson.why: Every Terraform codebase is built from four pieces. Most real incidents come from the seams between them: an unpinned provider upgrade, a data source read at the wrong time, or a module whose internals someone reached into. Interviewers use these to tell apart people who have run `terraform apply` from people who can own a shared codebase.
lesson.what: **Providers** are plugins that talk to an API (AWS, Kubernetes, or even your local disk). **Resources** are objects Terraform creates, updates and destroys, and records in state. **Data sources** only read existing information. **Modules** are directories of `.tf` files that you call with inputs and whose outputs you use, so that code can be reused.

concepts.name: Providers, versions and the lock file
concepts.body: `required_providers` gives each provider a source such as `hashicorp/aws` and a version constraint such as `~> 6.0`. `terraform init` selects versions and records them, with checksums, in `.terraform.lock.hcl`; later runs reuse that selection. Commit the lock file so upgrades go through review, and move within your constraints with `terraform init -upgrade`. The lock file tracks providers only, not modules.

concepts.name: Resources versus data sources
concepts.body: A `resource` block is managed: Terraform plans create, update or replace actions and stores the result in state. A `data` block is read-only: Terraform queries it during planning, but defers the read to apply when an argument depends on a value not known until apply. Use data sources to look up things you do not manage, such as an existing VPC or AMI, and never to 'import' something you intend to own.

concepts.name: Modules: inputs, outputs and versions
concepts.body: Every configuration is a root module; a `module` block calls a child module from `source`. Pass inputs as arguments and read results only through `module.<name>.<output>`, never by reaching into its resources. `version` is available only for registry modules. Because the lock file does not pin modules, a loose constraint can pull a newer module release on a fresh `init`, so use an exact version where reproducibility matters.

concepts.name: Provider configurations and aliases
concepts.body: A `provider` block configures a provider, for example a region. Add more configurations with `alias` and select one per resource with `provider = aws.west`, or pass one into a module with `providers = { aws = aws.west }`. The `version` argument inside a provider block is deprecated; put versions in `required_providers`. Keep credentials out of provider blocks and use environment, SSO or OIDC credentials instead.

e2e: You write configuration with `required_providers`, resources, data sources and module calls.
`terraform init` downloads providers that satisfy the constraints and writes `.terraform.lock.hcl`.
`terraform init` also installs child modules from their sources.
`terraform validate` checks the configuration's syntax and internal consistency.
`terraform plan` refreshes state, reads data sources and shows the difference from the desired configuration.
`terraform apply` creates, updates or replaces resources in dependency order and records them in state.
Outputs from modules and the root module expose selected values.
`terraform destroy` removes the managed resources; data sources never delete anything.

tasks.name: Initialise providers and read the lock file
tasks.goal: See exactly what `init` records and why it is committed.
steps: Install Terraform (or OpenTofu, using `tofu` instead of `terraform`). No cloud account is needed.
Run `terraform init` and open `.terraform.lock.hcl`: find the selected versions and the hashes.
Write one sentence on what would happen in CI if this file were not committed.

tasks.name: Compare a resource and a data source
tasks.goal: Tell managed objects from read-only lookups in a plan.
steps: Run `terraform plan`: note which blocks are create actions and that the `data` block is only read.
`terraform apply`, then `terraform state list`: the lookup is listed as `data.local_file.notes`. Explain why `terraform destroy` will never delete `notes.txt`.
Change `length = 2` to `3` and plan again: which resources are replaced, and why does `local_file` follow?
Delete `out/hello.txt` by hand and plan again. Explain what Terraform proposes.

tasks.name: Build and call a module
tasks.goal: Pass inputs in and read outputs out.
steps: Run `terraform init` again (new modules must be installed), then `terraform apply` and `terraform output messages`.
Explain why `version` cannot be added to this local `source`, and what you would use for a registry module.

tasks.name: Fix the broken configuration
tasks.goal: Diagnose the mistakes people make at the seams.
steps: A teammate wrote `source = "hashicorp/randomm"`: what does `init` report, and why?
Another added `version = "1.0.0"` to a module whose source is `./modules/greeting`.
A third referenced a resource inside the child module directly from the root instead of an output.
A fourth deleted `.terraform.lock.hcl` to 'fix' a checksum error. For each, give the error or risk and the fix.
Finish with `terraform destroy` to remove the local files.

key_terms: Provider — plugin that implements resources and data sources for one API.
`required_providers` — source address and version constraint per provider.
`.terraform.lock.hcl` — records selected provider versions and checksums; commit it.
Resource — managed object Terraform creates, updates, replaces and destroys.
Data source — read-only lookup; may be deferred to apply if inputs are unknown.
Module — directory of .tf files called with inputs and exposing outputs.
Provider alias — an additional provider configuration selected with `provider =`.
lesson.safety: The exercises use only the `random` and `local` providers, which never call a cloud API, so they are free and safe. If you try the same patterns with a cloud provider, use a sandbox account, read the plan before every apply and run `terraform destroy` afterwards.
cleanup: `terraform destroy` removes the local files created by the exercises.
Delete the practice folder, including `.terraform/` and the state files.
lesson.interview_question: After a routine pipeline run, `terraform plan` suddenly wants to replace several resources, although nobody changed the configuration. What could have changed between the two runs, and how would you design the codebase so this cannot happen silently?
interview_points: Provider version drift: lock file missing, not committed, or `init -upgrade` in CI.
Module version drift: a registry module with a loose constraint picked a newer release.
A data source now returns a different value (for example the latest AMI).
Real drift made outside Terraform, which the refresh detected.
Controls: commit the lock file, exact module versions, reviewed plans, pinned lookups.
lesson.reviewed_at: 2026-09-28 (checked against the official docs listed below)

iac/terraform-providers-resources-data-s.core:
**Core idea:** four building blocks, and most bugs live at the seams between them.
- **Provider**: plugin for an API. Pin it in `required_providers` (source + constraint). `terraform init` writes the selected version and checksums to `.terraform.lock.hcl`. Commit it; upgrade deliberately with `init -upgrade`.
- **Resource**: managed. Planned, applied, recorded in state, destroyable.
- **Data source**: read-only lookup, normally during plan. It is deferred to apply when an input is unknown until then.
- **Module**: a directory you call with inputs; read results only via `module.<name>.<output>`. `version` works only for registry modules, and the lock file does not pin modules.
- **Alias**: a second provider configuration (e.g. another region), selected with `provider = aws.west`.

Today's exercises use the `random` and `local` providers: real Terraform, zero cloud cost.

storyboard.title: Terraform: from configuration to managed state
storyboard.objective: Init installs providers that satisfy constraints and records them in the lock file.

scenes.title: Init selects providers
scenes.caption: Init installs providers that satisfy constraints and records them in the lock file.
scenes.narration: Terraform init reads required providers, installs matching versions and records the selection with checksums in the dependency lock file. Later runs reuse that selection until you upgrade deliberately.

scenes.title: Plan reads, then compares
scenes.caption: Data sources are read; resources are compared with state.
scenes.narration: Plan refreshes state and reads data sources, unless their inputs are unknown until apply. It then compares desired resources with recorded state and shows each create, update or replace.

scenes.title: Modules expose outputs
scenes.caption: The root module uses a child module only through its outputs.
scenes.narration: A child module receives inputs and exposes outputs. The root module uses those outputs, not the module's internal resources, so the module can change safely behind its interface.

scenes.title: Apply records state
scenes.caption: Apply changes resources in dependency order and saves the result.
scenes.narration: Apply performs the reviewed plan in dependency order and records every managed resource in state. Data sources are never managed, so destroy never deletes what they read.

lesson.title: Terraform state locking backends and drift
lesson.why: Concurrent infrastructure writers can corrupt decisions even when each configuration looks correct. State protection is part of change safety, not optional housekeeping.
lesson.what: Model remote state, locking, refresh, and drift reconciliation with no backend access.

concepts.name: State mapping
concepts.body: State connects Terraform resource addresses with remote object identities and recorded attributes. It can contain sensitive values even when outputs are marked sensitive. Restrict read access, encrypt storage, retain recoverable versions, and avoid committing state to Git.

concepts.name: Backend coordination
concepts.body: Backends store state and may support locking. Locking serializes cooperating operations against the same state; it does not lock all cloud APIs or prevent console changes. Verify the chosen backend's actual lock behavior rather than assuming remote means safe.

concepts.name: Drift detection
concepts.body: A refreshed plan compares configured intent with observed infrastructure and recorded state. Out-of-band changes can be adopted, reverted, or explicitly moved into another ownership model. A refresh-only operation changes recorded state, not configuration or remote objects.

concepts.name: Lock recovery
concepts.body: A stale lock may remain after interrupted execution. Confirm no writer is active and inspect operation ownership before unlocking. Force-unlocking a live operation enables concurrent writers and can invalidate both plans; a waiting lock is not itself evidence of failure.

e2e: A writer acquires the backend lock before protected state operations.
Refresh reads remote attributes and planning compares them with declared intent.
A reviewed decision accepts or reverses drift through the appropriate workflow.
State is updated and the lock released; independent manual changes remain possible.

tasks.name: Trace competing writers
steps: At 09:00 writer A holds the lock for state serial 12. Writer B arrives at 09:01 and waits. A completes serial 13 at 09:03; B must plan from 13, not reuse assumptions from 12. Expected result is serialized changes, not two simultaneous applies.

tasks.name: Classify a drift decision
steps: Configuration requests two replicas while a manual change sets four during an incident. Compare reverting to two, adopting four in code, and refreshing state only. Explain which choice changes service capacity and why refresh alone does not preserve four against future configured reconciliation.

tasks.name: Review backend access
steps: List who needs read, write, lock, and recovery access for a fictional backend. Separate CI writer permission from human audit reads. Include version recovery and explain why masking an output in terminal text does not remove its value from state.

tasks.name: Investigate a stale lock
steps: Given an old lock timestamp, check the associated job, host, and operation before declaring it abandoned. Record a recovery approval and state backup. Explain why elapsed time alone is insufficient when a provider operation legitimately takes longer than expected.

key_terms: State: mapping of addresses to remote objects.
Backend: state storage implementation.
Lock: cooperating-writer serialization.
Drift: difference between observed infrastructure and declared intent.
lesson.safety: Never fetch live state or unlock a real backend for this exercise.
cleanup: Discard the synthetic state timeline; no backend files were opened.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a pipeline reports a state lock after another job timed out. What must you verify before unlocking?
interview_points: Confirm the original writer actually stopped.
Inspect lock ownership and preserve recoverable state.
Replan after recovery rather than trusting stale assumptions.

storyboard.title: One state, one cooperating writer
storyboard.objective: Explain lock waiting and safe recovery.

scenes.title: Acquire ownership
scenes.caption: A owns the active operation.
scenes.narration: Writer A holds the state lock while refreshing and applying its reviewed changes.

scenes.title: Second writer waits
scenes.caption: Waiting is a safety mechanism.
scenes.narration: Writer B cannot safely update the same state while A remains active.

scenes.title: Release and replan
scenes.caption: Use the latest state.
scenes.narration: After A completes, B acquires the lock and plans from the updated state.

iac/terraform-state-locking-backends-and.core: State is sensitive ownership metadata. Backend locks serialize cooperating writers but not manual API changes. Diagnose lock ownership before recovery and review drift explicitly.

lesson.title: Terraform plans lifecycle dependencies and imports
lesson.why: A plan can be syntactically valid yet operationally disruptive. Dependency order, replacement behavior, and ownership imports need explicit review before execution.
lesson.what: Read a change graph and distinguish resource ordering, lifecycle controls, and import intent using an offline deployment model.

concepts.name: Plan evidence
concepts.body: Plans show proposed actions based on current configuration, inputs, state, and observations. Unknown values remain unresolved until execution. A saved plan captures a specific decision context; changed infrastructure or stale approvals can make blindly applying an old artifact inappropriate.

concepts.name: Dependency graph
concepts.body: Expression references usually establish dependencies automatically. Explicit depends_on handles real hidden dependencies but can broaden ordering and unknown values. Depending on an entire module when only one output matters may serialize unrelated work and make plans unnecessarily difficult to interpret.

concepts.name: Lifecycle trade-offs
concepts.body: create_before_destroy can reduce downtime when duplicate resources are allowed and quota exists. It cannot bypass uniqueness constraints. prevent_destroy guards some planned destruction while the configuration remains present; removing the resource block is not a durable external deletion protection.

concepts.name: Import and movement
concepts.body: Import binds existing remote objects to resource addresses; configuration still must describe intended management. A reviewed import plan may also propose changes, so import is not automatically read-only adoption. Address moves should use supported migration mechanisms to preserve identity rather than force replacement.

e2e: Configuration references establish the resource dependency graph.
Planning identifies creates, updates, replacements, imports, and unknown values.
Review checks destructive actions, lifecycle feasibility, and ownership agreements.
Execution follows dependencies, then state records the resulting object identities.

tasks.name: Calculate replacement headroom
steps: A service has three instances and quota allows four. Replacing one at a time with create-before-destroy can use four temporarily; replacing all three concurrently would require six and exceed quota by two. The expected safe sequence is bounded replacement with health checks between batches.

tasks.name: Trace an implicit edge
steps: A server consumes subnet.id from a network resource. Draw the implicit network-to-server dependency. Compare it with an explicit dependency on the entire networking module and identify unrelated logging resources that should not delay server planning or replacement.

tasks.name: Review an import
steps: An existing bucket has versioning enabled but proposed configuration omits the intended protection. Treat the import plan as an ownership and configuration review, not a ceremonial state update. Record the current setting and align code before approving any follow-up modification.

tasks.name: Investigate a rename
steps: A resource address changes from server.old to server.primary while its remote identifier is unchanged. Explain the apparent destroy/create risk without a move declaration. Document the old and new addresses, verify plan identity preservation, and discuss why renaming code should not silently replace a database.

key_terms: Plan: proposed infrastructure change set.
Dependency: required ordering relationship.
Replacement: new object substituted for old.
Import: mapping an existing object into management.
lesson.safety: Review fictional plans only; do not apply, import, move, or destroy real resources.
cleanup: Discard the graph and quota arithmetic; no state was modified.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a harmless resource rename produces a database replacement plan. How would you investigate and preserve identity?
interview_points: Compare addresses and remote identifiers.
Use supported address migration and replan.
Check replacement triggers and reject unintended destruction.

scenes.title: Plan overlap
scenes.caption: Both identities may coexist.
scenes.narration: Creating a replacement first requires capacity for the old and new instances.

scenes.title: Quota blocks creation
scenes.caption: Lifecycle cannot manufacture capacity.
scenes.narration: Insufficient quota prevents the replacement from starting while the old instance remains.

scenes.title: Bound the replacement batch
scenes.caption: Review health before retirement.
scenes.narration: A feasible batch creates healthy replacements before retiring corresponding old instances.

iac/terraform-plans-lifecycle-dependenci.core: Review plans as operational change graphs. Lifecycle settings have quota and uniqueness limits; imports establish ownership, and address migrations should preserve identity intentionally.

lesson.title: Terraform testing policy and sensitive outputs
lesson.why: Passing syntax checks does not prove safe infrastructure. Tests, policy checks, and secret handling cover different risks and require different evidence.
lesson.what: Layer configuration validation, mocked or real tests, plan policy, and controlled output handling without creating resources.

concepts.name: Validation layers
concepts.body: Formatting and validation catch structural problems but do not prove runtime permissions or service behavior. Variable validation, preconditions, and postconditions encode local contracts. Tests should exercise supported inputs and meaningful failures, not only assert that a plan can be produced.

concepts.name: Mocked versus real
concepts.body: Terraform tests can use plan or apply runs and supported provider mocking. Mocks are useful for deterministic logic but cannot prove cloud API behavior. Real apply tests need isolated accounts, budgets, ownership labels, and reliable cleanup rather than ordinary developer credentials.

concepts.name: Policy decisions
concepts.body: Plan policies check organization constraints such as allowed regions or prohibited public access. Unknown planned values require an explicit fail, defer, or exception policy. A rule that silently treats unknown as compliant creates a gap exactly where reviewers lack evidence.

concepts.name: Sensitive information
concepts.body: Sensitive markings reduce accidental display but do not automatically remove values from state or plan files. JSON output and artifact uploads can expose protected data. Restrict access and retention, redact logs, and prefer references to managed secrets over directly distributing secret values.

e2e: Static checks validate configuration shape and input contracts.
Tests exercise representative accepted and rejected cases.
A reviewed plan passes policy using explicit handling of unknown attributes.
Authorized execution and restricted artifacts preserve both change evidence and sensitive data.

tasks.name: Run a policy truth table
steps: Run python -c "cases=[('private',False),('public',True)]; print([name for name,is_public in cases if is_public])". Expected output is ['public']. This synthetic rule flags public exposure; add an unknown case on paper and decide whether missing evidence should block approval.

tasks.name: Design negative tests
tasks.goal: Test contracts rather than happy paths.
steps: For a module requiring replicas between one and five, list inputs zero, one, five, and six. Expect rejection, acceptance, acceptance, and rejection. Add an unsupported environment name and explain why successful formatting cannot detect this business constraint alone.

tasks.name: Assess mock coverage
steps: A mocked provider returns a healthy endpoint even when the real role lacks creation permission. Identify which assertion the mock can test and which needs an isolated integration test. Document cleanup ownership and a spending cap before any future real apply test.

tasks.name: Review artifact leakage
steps: A pipeline uploads a saved plan and JSON outputs to all repository readers. Identify potential sensitive fields, restrict artifact audience and lifetime, and publish only a redacted summary for review. Explain why a sensitive=true label does not make unrestricted plan storage safe.

key_terms: Precondition: requirement checked before an operation.
Mock: controlled substitute for provider behavior.
Policy: enforceable change constraint.
Sensitive output: display-protected value, not automatic encryption.
lesson.safety: Use synthetic booleans and numbers; do not generate plans containing live secrets.
cleanup: The local command creates no files; discard the fictional test matrix.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, all module tests pass but a deployment exposes a secret in an artifact. What did the validation strategy miss?
interview_points: Separate functional assertions from artifact confidentiality.
Inspect plan and output contents and access controls.
Add negative policy cases and explicit unknown handling.

storyboard.title: Tests and sensitive artifact controls solve different problems
storyboard.objective: Prevent a passing test from implying safe disclosure.

scenes.title: Tests pass
scenes.caption: Logic assertions are satisfied.
scenes.narration: The module passes its synthetic input and policy tests.

scenes.title: Artifact contains secrets
scenes.caption: Passing tests do not sanitize state.
scenes.narration: The saved plan may still contain sensitive values that must not be broadly shared.

scenes.title: Restrict and redact
scenes.caption: Share only necessary evidence.
scenes.narration: Authorized reviewers receive controlled artifacts while general logs contain a redacted summary.

iac/terraform-testing-policy-and-sensiti.core: Use layered tests and plan policies, distinguish mocks from integration evidence, handle unknown values explicitly, and protect state and plan artifacts despite sensitive markings.

lesson.title: OpenTofu infrastructure workflows and compatibility
lesson.why: A familiar command syntax does not make infrastructure engines interchangeable in every version. Migration needs tested state, provider, and language compatibility.
lesson.what: Plan an OpenTofu workflow and reversible migration using offline compatibility checks rather than switching production binaries blindly.

concepts.name: Workflow continuity
concepts.body: OpenTofu uses declarative configuration, providers, plans, and state, with familiar initialization and execution stages. Shared ancestry explains similarities but does not guarantee indefinite feature parity. Record exact engine versions and read compatibility notes for features your configuration actually uses.

concepts.name: Dependency compatibility
concepts.body: Providers, module sources, registry addresses, and lock files affect reproducibility. Verify required provider versions and supported platforms in a clean isolated copy. Changing the engine and upgrading providers simultaneously makes failures harder to attribute and complicates rollback analysis.

concepts.name: State protection
concepts.body: State format and optional encryption features impose compatibility requirements on every reader and writer. Enabling a feature that another engine cannot read may make a simple binary rollback impossible. Preserve protected backups and required keys, then test recovery before adoption.

concepts.name: Controlled migration
concepts.body: Use one authorized writer per environment, compare no-change plans where appropriate, and review every difference. A matching plan does not prove future provider operations will work, so combine static comparison with a bounded disposable integration test before high-impact adoption.

e2e: Inventory engine versions, dependencies, backends, and state features.
Validate a protected isolated copy without concurrent production writers.
Compare planned actions and investigate differences before approving migration.
Adopt one engine per state workflow and retain a tested recovery procedure.

tasks.name: Build a compatibility table
steps: Create columns for engine version, provider version, backend type, and state encryption. Hold the last three constant during the first engine comparison. Explain why a result from a newly upgraded provider cannot isolate an engine-only compatibility question.

tasks.name: Calculate migration coverage
steps: A team has twelve module scenarios. Nine produce reviewed equivalent plans, two expose unsupported features, and one has not run. Verified coverage is 9/12=75 percent, not 100 percent of completed successes. The three unresolved scenarios block a claim of complete compatibility.

tasks.name: Design recovery evidence
steps: List the previous engine binary version, protected state snapshot, provider lock data, and any encryption keys as recovery dependencies. Describe a read-and-plan restore check using a disposable copy. Explain why possessing a backup without its decryption capability is insufficient.

tasks.name: Diagnose a changed plan
tasks.goal: Avoid treating every difference as drift.
steps: A comparison proposes replacement only after both engine and provider upgrades. Freeze the provider to its original compatible version in the isolated model and compare again. Classify remaining differences as language, provider, state, or real remote changes before accepting destructive actions.

key_terms: OpenTofu: open-source infrastructure-as-code engine.
Compatibility: supported behavior across chosen versions.
Lock file: recorded dependency selections.
State encryption: protection requiring compatible readers and keys.
lesson.safety: Do not open or convert production state; use inventories and synthetic comparison results.
cleanup: Discard the fictional matrix; preserve all existing binaries and state unchanged.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, your team wants to replace Terraform with OpenTofu in every pipeline tomorrow. What evidence would you require first?
interview_points: Check exact language, provider, backend, and state compatibility.
Compare isolated plans with one migration variable at a time.
Prove recovery and prevent concurrent mixed-engine writers.

storyboard.title: Compatibility is a tested matrix, not a name change

scenes.title: Hold dependencies steady
scenes.caption: Change one variable first.
scenes.narration: An isolated comparison retains known provider and backend settings.

scenes.title: Find incompatibility
scenes.caption: Unexpected replacement blocks adoption.
scenes.narration: A differing plan requires explanation before the new engine can own the state.

scenes.title: Prove and adopt
scenes.caption: One writer and tested recovery.
scenes.narration: Reviewed compatibility and recovery evidence permit a controlled workflow transition.

iac/opentofu-infrastructure-workflows-an.core: Verify exact engine, provider, backend, and state compatibility. Compare protected copies, change one variable at a time, and prove recovery before migrating state ownership.

lesson.title: Pulumi infrastructure programming and state
lesson.why: General-purpose languages improve abstraction but also introduce runtime and dependency behavior. Infrastructure side effects still require explicit state and execution controls.
lesson.what: Connect Pulumi programs, stacks, deferred outputs, previews, and secret propagation without creating a cloud stack.

concepts.name: Program evaluation
concepts.body: A Pulumi program registers desired resources with the deployment engine. Ordinary language execution and resource operations are not identical; side effects outside resource APIs can run during evaluation. Keep previews free of uncontrolled external writes and pin language dependencies alongside providers.

concepts.name: Deferred outputs
concepts.body: Resource outputs may be unknown during preview and resolve after creation. Output transformations preserve dependency information rather than turning cloud values into immediate ordinary strings. Avoid assuming a future endpoint is available when the program first evaluates its declarations.

concepts.name: Stack isolation
concepts.body: Stacks hold configuration and state for independent instances of a program. Separate names alone do not guarantee separate credentials, accounts, or permissions. Protect the state backend and define clear ownership so staging code cannot accidentally receive production authority.

concepts.name: Secrets and previews
concepts.body: Pulumi tracks secret values and can propagate secrecy through derived outputs, using configured encryption mechanisms for state. Logging plaintext or sending it through unrelated libraries can still leak it. Preview shows proposed changes but cannot guarantee every runtime API call will succeed.

e2e: A selected stack supplies reviewed configuration and scoped credentials.
Program evaluation registers resources and deferred dependencies with the engine.
Preview presents proposed changes, including values that remain unknown.
Approved execution resolves outputs and records state while protecting secret-marked values.

tasks.name: Evaluate ordinary code
steps: Run python -c "envs={'dev':1,'prod':3}; print(sum(envs.values()))". Expected output is 4. This computes a desired replica total without provisioning anything. Explain why constructing a Pulumi resource with that count would introduce engine-managed lifecycle beyond the plain calculation.

tasks.name: Trace a deferred endpoint
steps: Draw a database resource whose hostname feeds an application configuration output. Mark the hostname unknown during an initial preview. Explain why converting it into a guessed string breaks the intended dependency and why output transformations should avoid unrelated irreversible side effects.

tasks.name: Review stack boundaries
steps: Compare dev and production stacks that share a program but use different accounts and state access. Specify which CI identity may update each. Include a review of selected-stack context before execution and reject the assumption that a stack name alone enforces isolation.

tasks.name: Investigate secret leakage
steps: A secret-marked database password is printed by a helper library during evaluation. Identify the leak path despite protected state. Replace plaintext logging with a nonsecret connection identifier, audit retained logs, and document rotation requirements if a real credential were ever exposed.

key_terms: Stack: independent configured program instance.
Output: deferred value with dependency metadata.
Preview: proposed resource-change evaluation.
Secret propagation: preserving sensitivity through derived values.
lesson.safety: Use only local arithmetic; no Pulumi login, credentials, stack creation, or update is required.
cleanup: The command creates no files or resources; discard the dependency sketch.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a Pulumi preview unexpectedly sends an external notification. Why is that risky, and how would you redesign the program?
interview_points: Separate language side effects from engine-managed resources.
Keep preview evaluation free of irreversible external writes.
Use explicit post-deployment steps with scoped authorization.

storyboard.title: Deferred outputs carry resource dependencies
storyboard.objective: Distinguish preview values from resolved infrastructure.

scenes.title: Preview registration
scenes.caption: The endpoint may be unknown.
scenes.narration: The program registers a database whose hostname is not yet available.

scenes.title: Premature assumption
scenes.caption: A guessed string loses the contract.
scenes.narration: Application configuration cannot safely depend on an invented endpoint during initial preview.

scenes.title: Resolve dependencies
scenes.caption: Outputs carry the real value.
scenes.narration: Execution resolves the hostname and its dependency into the application configuration.

iac/pulumi-infrastructure-programming-an.core: Pulumi evaluates programs but manages resources through an engine. Preserve deferred output dependencies, isolate stack authority, and keep previews and logs free of unsafe side effects.

lesson.title: Ansible inventory roles playbooks and idempotency
lesson.why: Fleet automation becomes dangerous when target selection or repeated execution is unclear. Idempotent intent should reduce surprises rather than hide unbounded commands.
lesson.what: Model inventory targeting, playbook tasks, roles, handlers, and check-mode limitations using a local configuration example.

concepts.name: Inventory scope
concepts.body: Inventory defines hosts, groups, and variables used to select targets. Group membership and variable precedence can change effective behavior unexpectedly. Always preview the intended host set and separate production inventory from practice so a broad pattern cannot silently expand blast radius.

concepts.name: Declarative modules
concepts.body: Modules often express desired state, such as a package being present or a file having specific content. Arbitrary shell commands do not automatically inherit idempotency. Register results and define change or failure conditions only when they accurately represent the command's real effects.

concepts.name: Roles and handlers
concepts.body: Roles package related tasks, defaults, templates, and handlers behind reusable interfaces. Handlers typically run when notified by changed tasks and consolidate repeated notifications. A configuration write should notify a service reload only when content actually changes and validation has succeeded.

concepts.name: Check and diff
concepts.body: Check mode predicts supported changes without ordinary mutation, but support varies by module and task. Diff can reveal sensitive file contents. A clean check run is not proof of runtime success; combine limited target execution, assertions, and a second idempotency run.

e2e: Inventory selection identifies the exact hosts and effective variables.
Tasks converge supported resources toward declared configuration.
Changed validated content notifies a bounded reload handler.
A second run reports no unnecessary changes, while assertions verify the service still works.

tasks.name: Simulate convergence
tasks.goal: Run a safe local state calculation.
steps: Run python -c "current={'mode':'old'}; desired={'mode':'safe'}; print(current!=desired, desired!=desired)". Expected output is True False. The first comparison requires change; the second is already converged. Explain how this differs from a shell task that always appends another line.

tasks.name: Audit target scope
steps: Create fictional groups staging={s1,s2} and production={p1,p2,p3}. A staging limit selects two hosts, while all selects five. Record the expected host count before any future run and identify shared variables that should not carry production credentials into staging.

tasks.name: Design a reload path
steps: Describe rendering a service configuration, validating its syntax, installing it only when different, and notifying one reload handler. Explain why reloading after failed validation is unsafe and why two changed templates should not trigger two unnecessary identical reloads.

tasks.name: Diagnose false idempotency
steps: A shell task modifies a file on every run but declares changed_when=false. Explain why the green report hides mutation rather than making the task idempotent. Replace the action conceptually with a state-aware module and verify both content and second-run change counts.

key_terms: Inventory: host and variable targeting data.
Playbook: ordered automation plays and tasks.
Role: reusable task and configuration package.
Handler: change-triggered deferred task.
lesson.safety: Run only the supplied local calculation; do not contact SSH hosts or use privilege escalation.
cleanup: No files or remote changes are created; discard the fictional inventory.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a playbook reports no changes but restarts a service every run. How would you investigate its idempotency?
interview_points: Inspect shell side effects and change reporting.
Use state-aware modules and validated handler notifications.
Verify actual state and a second bounded execution.

storyboard.title: Changed configuration should trigger one validated reload

scenes.title: Detect a real difference
scenes.caption: Desired content differs.
scenes.narration: The task validates and installs changed configuration.

scenes.title: Reject invalid content
scenes.caption: Validation failure must not reload.
scenes.narration: A malformed candidate blocks installation and should not trigger a service restart.

scenes.title: Converge cleanly
scenes.caption: A second run needs no reload.
scenes.narration: After valid configuration is installed, repeated evaluation finds no further change.

iac/ansible-inventory-roles-playbooks-an.core: Preview inventory scope, prefer state-aware modules, notify handlers only on validated change, and prove idempotency with actual state plus a second run.

lesson.title: Configuration drift patching and immutable infrastructure
lesson.why: Unrecorded fixes make machines unique and recovery uncertain. Patching must reduce exposure without creating an unrepeatable fleet.
lesson.what: Compare in-place convergence with image replacement and design a drift response that preserves urgent repairs in durable source.

concepts.name: Drift classification
concepts.body: Drift is a difference between declared and observed state, not automatically malicious activity. Classify emergency repairs, unauthorized changes, and harmless observations separately. Decide whether to adopt or reverse each change and record ownership so competing automation does not repeatedly undo approved work.

concepts.name: Mutable patching
concepts.body: In-place updates can quickly address a narrow package issue without rebuilding every machine. They leave more historical variation and may require reboots or service restarts. Verify package provenance, dependency changes, maintenance windows, and post-patch health rather than counting installation success alone.

concepts.name: Immutable replacement
concepts.body: Image-based replacement builds a tested artifact and replaces instances instead of repairing each one indefinitely. It improves reproducibility but requires build pipelines, spare capacity, state separation, and rollout control. Persistent data must not exist only on a disposable instance root disk.

concepts.name: Convergence and exceptions
concepts.body: Emergency exceptions need expiration, owner, and a path back into code or images. Drift detection should produce actionable evidence rather than silently overwrite everything. A rollback artifact must remain compatible with external data and current security requirements before it is considered safe.

e2e: Compare declared configuration with observed fleet state and classify differences.
Choose a patch or replacement path based on urgency and operational constraints.
Test a bounded cohort and verify service behavior plus required security changes.
Promote the durable configuration and close temporary exceptions after convergence.

tasks.name: Calculate rollout waves
steps: A fleet has ten instances and may replace two per wave while maintaining eight. Five waves are required. If each wave takes six minutes including health checks, the ideal sequential duration is thirty minutes. Failed checks stop the sequence rather than being excluded from the estimate.

tasks.name: Classify an emergency fix
steps: An operator changes a timeout from two to five seconds during an outage. Compare the live value with code and record why the change helped. Decide whether to test and adopt five or revert; avoid an automatic reconciliation loop that toggles the value without review.

tasks.name: Design an immutable boundary
steps: List application binaries, package versions, logs, uploaded files, and database records. Put reproducible binaries in the image and define external durable stores for irreplaceable state. Explain why replacing a server with local uploads is not a safe immutable rollout.

tasks.name: Plan patch verification
tasks.goal: Check outcomes rather than command success.
steps: For a fictional library patch, verify the loaded runtime version, restart requirement, synthetic transaction, and rollback compatibility. A package manager success code alone does not prove a long-running process loaded the patched library. Record the exact artifact and evidence for later audit.

key_terms: Drift: observed divergence from declared state.
Mutable patch: updating an existing host.
Immutable rollout: replacing hosts with a built artifact.
Exception: bounded deviation with an owner and expiry.
lesson.safety: Use a fictional fleet; never patch shared hosts or remove their local data during practice.
cleanup: Discard the rollout table; no package or image changes were made.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, an emergency patch fixed production but the next image rollout reintroduced the bug. What process change prevents recurrence?
interview_points: Record the emergency change with owner and expiry.
Rebuild and test the durable source artifact.
Verify loaded versions and close drift only after convergence.

storyboard.title: An emergency repair must reach the source artifact
storyboard.objective: Prevent a later rollout from undoing a fix.

scenes.title: Repair urgently
scenes.caption: One host now differs from source.
scenes.narration: An emergency patch restores the instance but creates an intentional configuration difference.

scenes.title: Old image threatens regression
scenes.caption: A local fix is not durable source.
scenes.narration: Replacing hosts from the unchanged image would reintroduce the original defect.

scenes.title: Promote the durable fix
scenes.caption: Test and rebuild before rollout.
scenes.narration: The reviewed repair enters the image and reaches the fleet through bounded replacement.

iac/configuration-drift-patching-and-imm.core: Classify drift, choose mutable patching or immutable replacement deliberately, and feed emergency repairs into durable source. Verify loaded runtime state, not just installation status.

lesson.title: Infrastructure promotion environment isolation and rollback
lesson.why: A tested change can still fail when promoted with different inputs or excessive authority. Environment boundaries and rollback semantics must be designed before release.
lesson.what: Promote reviewed infrastructure intent while preserving separate state, credentials, configuration, and evidence for each environment.

concepts.name: Promotion unit
concepts.body: Promote a versioned module or configuration commit together with explicit dependency and artifact versions. Environment values may differ intentionally, but rebuilding or resolving floating dependencies during each stage weakens evidence that production matches what staging tested.

concepts.name: Isolation layers
concepts.body: Separate state reduces accidental cross-environment ownership, while separate credentials and accounts constrain authority. Workspaces or directories alone are not a complete security boundary. Backend access, network access, and deployment identity must all match the selected target environment.

concepts.name: Environment-specific plans
concepts.body: Generate and review a plan against each environment's own state and inputs. A staging plan artifact is not a production change plan. Approval must bind to the actual proposed actions, source revision, identity, and target, especially for replacements or destructive changes.

concepts.name: Rollback limits
concepts.body: Reverting code expresses previous intent but does not guarantee reversible infrastructure or data changes. Deleted storage, incompatible schemas, and identity rotation may require restore or forward repair. Keep a tested recovery route and understand which changes cross irreversible boundaries.

e2e: Build a versioned change and validate it in a low-risk environment.
Select the target's independent state, inputs, and scoped identity.
Review that target's plan with compatibility and recovery evidence.
Apply approved intent, verify service behavior, and retain the exact release record.

tasks.name: Calculate blast radius
steps: One deployment identity can update three environments with eight resources each: its potential managed scope is twenty-four resources. Separate identities limited to one environment reduce each identity's scope to eight. This arithmetic models scope only; resource criticality and indirect privileges still matter.

tasks.name: Define a promotion manifest
steps: Record module commit, provider lock digest, image digest, and nonsecret environment input version for a fictional release. Distinguish values that must remain identical from intentional production differences such as replica count. Explain why an unrecorded latest-image lookup defeats that record.

tasks.name: Review target selection
tasks.goal: Prevent valid changes in the wrong environment.
steps: A pipeline selects production credentials but a staging state key. Describe the dangerous mismatch and add explicit checks for account, backend key, and approved environment before planning. Do not rely solely on a friendly workspace name displayed in a job title.

tasks.name: Build a recovery decision
steps: A change replaces a stateless worker and removes a database column. Reverting the worker digest may be easy; the deleted column requires compatibility analysis and a recoverable data source. Split these changes into safer stages and define a stop gate before irreversible cleanup.

key_terms: Promotion: moving reviewed intent between environments.
Isolation: separating authority and state boundaries.
Release record: immutable change evidence.
Forward repair: correcting state without reverting all changes.
lesson.safety: Use synthetic identities and plans; do not switch real backends or execute infrastructure changes.
cleanup: Discard the fictional release manifest; existing state and credentials remain untouched.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, staging passed but production requires replacing a database. How should promotion approval and recovery planning change?
interview_points: Review the production-specific plan and inputs.
Check target identity and state isolation.
Require data compatibility and restore evidence before destructive actions.

storyboard.title: Promote intent, not another environment's plan
storyboard.objective: Keep target state and authority aligned.

scenes.title: Validate the release
scenes.caption: Staging supplies its own inputs.
scenes.narration: The versioned change is tested against staging state and scoped authority.

scenes.title: Production differs
scenes.caption: Its plan needs separate review.
scenes.narration: Production inputs expose a replacement not present in staging, so approval pauses.

scenes.title: Approve target-specific intent
scenes.caption: Recovery evidence accompanies approval.
scenes.narration: A reviewed production plan and compatible recovery route permit controlled promotion.

iac/infrastructure-promotion-environment.core: Promote immutable intent and dependencies, but generate target-specific plans. Separate state and authority, verify target identity, and distinguish code rollback from data recovery.
